https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62q.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The last time it was confirmed that part of a rocket had collided with the Moon by accident was in 2022 By Pallab Ghosh Science Correspondent Published 2 hours ago A stray SpaceX rocket is believed to have crashed into the Moon, forming a crater near a famous lunar landmark and giving scientists a unique research opportunity that could help future missions. The empty upper stage of a Falcon 9 rocket was due to strike the Moon near the Einstein crater at a speed of about 5,400mph (8,700km/h) on Wednesday. The short, dramatic flash it created would have been hard to catch by amateur astronomers even with high-end telescopes, but larger observatories in the Americas are analysing the information. It could be days or even weeks before the full picture of what happened and what we can learn from it is known - but for planetary geologists, this accidental collision is a scientific gift. Figure caption, Watch: Science Museum's head of space on what scientists will look for after crash Space X's Falcon 9 rocket is a reusable model and has been sent into space on several missions. Its design allows part of the rocket to return to Earth, but other sections are shed in space. The rocket blasted off from Florida in January last year, carrying two lunar landers into space. Its job was to fire the upper stage hard enough to send both of the landers out of Earth's orbit and onto a path towards the Moon - mission accomplished. The spent stage - which is about the size of a five-storey building and weighs at least 4,000kg - was left drifting in a long, looping orbit that swung out towards the Moon and back again. Over the next 18 months, the gentle gravitational tug of the Earth, Moon and Sun, along with even light from the Sun, gave a faint push. Astronomers tracking the rocket part eventually worked out that those small nudges had put it on a course towards the Moon and was picking up speed every day. The impact at around 07:35 BST (06:35 GMT) on Wednesday happened in broad daylight for many parts of the world, but the tiny flash it produced would have been far too faint to see, even through a telescope. Amateur astronomers observing in darkness would also have had little realistic chance of seeing the flash, given that it would have lasted a fraction of a second. But they may have seen a plume of dust stretching as far as 100km (62 miles) that lasted for several minutes. Even spacecraft orbiting the Moon were not in the right place at the right time to watch the impact happen live. South Korea's Danuri orbiter had the best chance, having passed near the crash site shortly beforehand. Its team has told Korean media that any footage will only be released once researchers have completed their analysis. Over the next few days, Nasa's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter will be in position to photograph the site, allowing images before and after the crash to be compared. Image source, NASA Image caption, The Einstein crater is over 180km (112 miles) wide, and is large enough to contain a smaller crater inside The science and probably the first images will come from powerful telescopes in the Americas where the sky was still dark. Even then, turning the detection of a 14m object hitting the lunar surface 385,000km away won't be easy. Image processing to clean up the picture can take hours, days or even weeks, as scientists check and process the data. Because researchers already know the rocket's exact size, speed and point of impact, this collision turns from being a random accident into a rare, controlled experiment. It is a dream moment for planetary scientists because it lets them test their models of how impacts dig out craters, throw debris across the surface, and send tremors through the Moon's interior. That has real practical value. Understanding how much rock and dust an impact throws up will help engineers design safer landers and future Moon bases, working out how far flying debris can travel and how hard the ground might shake nearby. Material thrown up from beneath the surface offers fresh clues about the Moon's geology, adding to what scientists already know about how the Earth-Moon system formed some 4.5 billion years ago. This is not the first time a human-made object has struck the Moon. Since 1959, dozens of spacecraft have crashed into it, some by accident and many deliberately for science. The Soviet probe Luna 2 was the first, followed over the decades by Nasa's Ranger probes in the 1960s, several Apollo-era rocket stages, and more recently the LCROSS mission in 2009, which was deliberately crashed to search for water ice. The last confirmed accidental impact , in 2022, was thought to be the leftover booster from a Chinese lunar mission launched back in 2014 - a reminder that this sort of space debris has been quietly piling up above our heads for well over half a century. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce9e.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ursula von der Leyen and Mark Rutte accused Russia of becoming increasingly reckless in its attacks on Europe By Paul Kirby Europe digital editor Published 2 September 2026, 14:04 BST Updated 3 hours ago The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal". "Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack last month on Leipzig airport. "We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better," von der Leyen said. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the whole alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany". Russia has rejected German accusations that a drone carrying explosives deliberately targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August. The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane. A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents. The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations. Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Russian House in Berlin is to close as part of Germany's response to the Leipzig incident Berlin has said it will close the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as the Russian House cultural institution, widely suspected in Berlin of acting as a propaganda outlet for the Kremlin. The Russian foreign ministry promised to respond in "mirror-image" fashion and said Berlin had offered no evidence to back its claims. Germany's chargÃ© d'affaires Bernd Finke was summoned to hear Moscow's rejection of Berlin's "entirely unfounded accusations". Vladimir Putin has condemned Germany's measures as a serious mistake that "clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people". Asked whether Moscow would be prepared to sever relations with Berlin, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko answered "maybe", but said for now it was giving diplomacy a chance. Critics in Germany suggested the German response was relatively weak, but Berlin has its eye on a more co-ordinated response with its allies, including extended EU sanctions and entry restrictions on Russian visitors across the bloc. Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West Published 8 hours ago Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack Published 18 hours ago Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations Published 4 hours ago Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil". "We will not tolerate it," she said. While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions. Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack. Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said they were working on how to tighten enforcement of existing sanctions, and added there was broad support for an EU visa entry ban on Russian ex-combatants as well as stricter visa limits on Russian tourists. Several EU countries, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, are pushing for more than â¬193bn (Â£165bn) in frozen Russian assets to be used to help Ukraine. The idea was first planned at the end of 2025, and rejected by Belgium where the money is held. However, Belgium's position is unchanged because it fears being held financially liable by the courts. The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said. Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig". Image source, Reuters Image caption, Police search an area in Bergheim after an attack on a substation Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne. Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole. "We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said. Several power lines failed prompting five power plant units to go offline at two separate coal-fired power stations. Police said six launching devices had been found in a field. High-voltage power lines were damaged near the JÃ¤nschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg early on Tuesday and explosive devices were later found at a substation. Meanwhile, in neighbouring Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a fire at a factory producing combat drones at SkarÅ¼ysko-Kamienna, 140km (85 miles) south of Warsaw was a deliberate act of arson and sabotage. Arson has also not been ruled out in a fire at a factory in Lublin on Sunday night. Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest". The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine â¬90bn (Â£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added. She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent children, men and children in Ukraine". http://www.bgnes.com/weather/less-snowfa.text: Winter in Europe could bring an unwelcome surprise: three-month seasonal models suggest above-average temperatures across most of the continent, with snowfall projected to be less frequent than normal. The highest probability of snow remains confined to Northern Europe and high-altitude Alpine regions, reports Romanian outlet Libertatea. Winter conditions will be influenced by a Super El Niño and a potential weakening of the polar vortex starting in late December. Seasonal climate models, however, reflect general trends and cannot pinpoint isolated cold snaps or individual snow events. December 2026 Outlook Much of Europe is forecast to see higher-than-normal temperatures, driven by prevailing westerly winds delivering warm, humid Atlantic air masses. January 2027 Outlook Conditions will largely remain mild through January. Shifts in atmospheric circulation remain possible over northern parts of the continent, and Atlantic low-pressure systems could periodically push precipitation and cold air inward. February Outlook In February, Northern Europe could return to near-normal seasonal averages, whereas southern reaches of the continent are expected to stay relatively mild. Even so, cold air intrusions cannot be entirely ruled out, as much will depend on the trajectory of cyclones and broader atmospheric changes. Where Snow Is Most Likely Forecasters anticipate below-average snowfall across most European territories. Favorable conditions for snow cover will be concentrated in northern latitudes and high mountain ranges, particularly the Alps. While incoming Atlantic air masses will carry abundant moisture, precipitation will not necessarily fall as snow without sufficiently low surface temperatures. Above-average snow totals are possible at elevations exceeding 1,800–2,000 meters in the Alps should cold conditions hold. Given the shortage of natural snow at lower altitudes, some European ski resorts may struggle to maintain optimal ski conditions. How the Polar Vortex Could Affect Winter Weather Meteorologists caution that the polar vortex is likely to weaken significantly beginning in late December. A disrupted vortex can heighten the chances of cold Arctic air spilling down into mid-latitudes. However, a weakening polar vortex does not guarantee freezing temperatures or snowfall for any specific country, as winter weather across Europe also hinges heavily on North Atlantic circulation patterns and related atmospheric factors. | BGNES
